written.myAnswer: Crossing over exchanges genetic material between homologous chromosomes, creating new combinations of genes. This increases genetic variation in the gametes.
In prophase-I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair by synapsis, form tetrads, and may undergo crossing over. These events do not occur in prophase of mitosis.
Meiosis halves the chromosome number, producing haploid cells from a diploid parent cell. Mitosis maintains the chromosome number.
Sister chromatids are the two identical chromatids joined at the centromere in a replicated chromosome. They separate during anaphase-II of meiosis.

In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair to form tetrads and crossing over may occur. In metaphase-I, tetrads align at the equator. In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles. In telophase-I, chromosomes reach the poles, nuclei may reform, and cytokinesis divides the cell into two haploid cells.

Meiosis produces haploid reproductive cells, so fertilization restores the diploid chromosome number in the zygote and helps maintain chromosome number across generations. Crossing over and the independent assortment of chromosomes also create genetic variation.
